newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says screen workers have right to eye exams.
newsitem.headline: Court says screen workers have right to eye exams.

text.p: Member states should be given broad discretion in interpreting a provision in Community rules on eye examinations for workers who "habitually use display screen equipment as a significant part of their normal work", the European Court of Justice has ruled.
The court noted in a ruling issued on Thursday that Directive 90/270/EEC did not define the phrase.
"In view of the vagueness of the pharse in issue, the Member States must be accorded a broad discretion when adopting such implementing measures..." it said.
The court also said the rules required ophthalmological examinations in all cases where an eye and eyesight test carried out under provisions of the directive showed it was necessary.
It also said the directive applied to all workstations as defined by the directive, even if they were not used by workers habitually as a significant part of their work.
Community rules "require employers to take appropriate steps to ensure that workstations meet the minimum requirements ...for equipment, environment and operator/computer interface," the court said.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: Italian)

"Directive 90/270/EEC on the minimum safety and health requirements for work with display screen equipment - Definition of worker - Eye and Eyesight tests - Definition of workstation for the purposes of artices 4 and 5 - Extent of the obligations laid down in article 4 and 5"
References by the Procura della Repubblica presso la Pretura Circondariale di Torino, Italy and by the Pretura Circondariale di Torino, for a preliminary ruling in the criminal proceedings against

on the interpretation of Council directive 90/270/EEC of 29 May 1990 on the minimum safety and health requirements for work with display screen equipment (fifth individual directive within the meaning of article 16(1) of directive 89/391/EEC)(OJ 19990 L 156, p. 14)
Declares that the questions referred to it by the Procura della Repubblica presso la Pretura Circondariale di Torino are inadmissible;
in answer to the questions referred by the Pretura Circondariale di Torino, by order of 18 April 1995, rules

1. Article 9(1) of Council directive 90/270/EEC of 29 May 1990 on the minimum safety and health requirements for work with display screen equipment (fifth individual directive within the meaning of article 16(1) of directive 89/391/EEC) must be interpreted as meaning that the regular eye tests for which it provides are to be carried out on all workers to whom the directive applies and article 9(2) is to be interpreted as meaning that workers are entitled to an ophthalmological examination in all cases where the eye and eyesight test carried out pursuant to article 9(1) shows that this is necessary.

2. On a proper construction of articles 4 and 5 of directive 90/270, the obligations they impose apply to all workstations as defined in article 2(b), even if they are not used by workers as defined in article 2(c), and workstations must be adapted to comply with all the minimum requirements laid down in the Annex.
